question: My dog gets restless when fasting but I don't want to break the fast — what can I give?
answer: A frozen bone broth ball is the perfect trick. Pour plain, unsalted bone broth into an ice cube tray or silicone mold, freeze it, and give one when your dog is restless. It satisfies the urge to have 'something' and takes time to lick, but it's so low in calories and carbs that it barely disrupts the fasting benefits — no real insulin spike, and the gut still gets its rest. It's a holistic favorite for exactly this situation: a restless faster who needs a little something without truly breaking the fast.
source: Common Sense Dog — Fasting & Bone Broth pack

question: Does bone broth break a dog's fast?
answer: Only minimally. Plain bone broth is very low in calories and carbohydrates, so it doesn't cause the insulin spike or heavy digestive load that real food does — which means most of the fasting benefits (gut rest, low insulin, cellular cleanup) stay largely intact. It's considered a 'clean' near-fast option rather than a true meal. Keep it plain and unsalted with no onion or garlic broth bases, and it's a gentle way to support a fasting dog without derailing it.
source: Common Sense Dog — Fasting & Bone Broth pack

question: Why would I fast my dog, and is it healthy?
answer: Short, intermittent fasting (for example skipping a meal or doing a longer overnight gap) gives the digestive system a rest, helps lower insulin, and supports the body's natural cleanup and repair processes — it's part of the holistic 'constant cleansing' idea. Many healthy adult dogs do well on it, and dogs in the wild naturally ate this way rather than grazing all day. That said, fasting is NOT for puppies, pregnant or nursing dogs, diabetic dogs, or very small/toy breeds prone to low blood sugar. When in doubt, check with a holistic vet before starting.
source: Common Sense Dog — Fasting & Bone Broth pack

question: How do I make a frozen bone broth treat for my dog?
answer: It's easy: use plain, unsalted bone broth (homemade or a clean store-bought one with no onion, garlic, or added salt), pour it into an ice cube tray, silicone mold, or a lick-friendly toy, and freeze. Give one when your dog needs something to do or is restless during a fast. For extra enrichment you can freeze it in a stuffable toy so it lasts longer. It's hydrating, gut-supporting, and low-impact enough to use during fasting windows.
source: Common Sense Dog — Fasting & Bone Broth pack

question: What are the benefits of bone broth for dogs?
answer: Bone broth is one of the best whole-food additions you can give. It's rich in collagen, gelatin, and glycine that support the gut lining (great for leaky gut and digestion), plus it supplies joint-supporting compounds and is wonderfully hydrating and palatable. It's gentle enough for sick, recovering, or fasting dogs, and a great way to get fluids and nutrition into a dog that's off its food. Keep it plain and unsalted, with no onion or garlic, and it fits virtually any holistic diet.
source: Common Sense Dog — Fasting & Bone Broth pack

question: What treats can I give during a dog's fasting window without ruining it?
answer: Stick to very low-calorie, low-carb options that don't trigger a real digestive or insulin response. A frozen plain bone broth ball is the top pick — satisfying, hydrating, and barely disruptive. Plain water with a splash of bone broth, or a few licks of broth, work too. Avoid starchy biscuits, anything sugary, and calorie-dense chews during the fast, since those genuinely break it. The goal is to occupy a restless dog while keeping the gut rest and low-insulin benefits intact.
source: Common Sense Dog — Fasting & Bone Broth pack
